html:
PhD in acoustics.

In one sentence: recreating, in a virtual world, the soundscape of a car driving past in the real world.

A bit more specifically: record car pass-by noise with a microphone array, extract the positions and signals of the moving sources, then reconstruct those positions and signals in a virtual world, so that someone listening over headphones or loudspeakers hears the same car pass-by as in the real world. This process, from simulation to what the ear actually hears, is called auralization.

In more detail:

  1. Simulating the sound field of moving sources. Since beamforming would later be used to extract the data, the simulation also had to remove the Doppler effect from the recorded signals;
  2. Designing the microphone array. Post-processing used both delay-and-sum beamforming and compressive beamforming, so the array design was optimized for both.
  3. Car pass-by experiments. With the simulations and arrays ready, I ran two rounds of pass-by measurements on a test track, testing three arrays in all. For validation, the car carried a loudspeaker playing a known signal.
  4. Synthesizing source signals of any length. Because the source is moving, the analysis windows have to be very short so as not to compromise spatial resolution, which means the extracted signals can’t be played back directly. Tonal components are fairly simple: find the amplitude and frequency and synthesize them directly. For the noise part, convolving the signal recovered by beamforming with white noise also gives you any length you want.

From there, auralization takes two more steps: a sound propagation model (using geometric or numerical methods, for example) and a reproduction technique (binaural HRTFs over headphones, say, or Ambisonics or CTC over loudspeakers). I won’t go into those here; I’ll cover them in detail in my column later:

Acoustics: Tech You Can Hear

If I had to name a contribution, it would be extending beamforming to auralization. In auralization, synthesizing simple, static sources is no longer a problem, but few people work on complex and moving sources. Switzerland’s Empa does a lot on moving sources, but its models are built entirely on theoretical and empirical formulas, so the realism of the synthesized sound leaves room for improvement.

In practice, this can be used to predict how different urban planning options will sound to residents (I’m not saying “noise” here, because besides decibels there are many other measures of how annoying people find a sound, and the most accurate assessment is subjective: let people listen for themselves), as well as for urban sound design, noise management and so on. When I visited Arup in the Netherlands last year, I saw they had already started using it in real projects, letting residents and decision-makers hear the difference a noise barrier makes. Everyone was very happy with the result, because if you just show them dB values, they don’t believe you. It was gratifying to see the field I work in being put to real use, even though it wasn’t my technology, haha.

I won’t go into publications and the like; mine can’t compare with those of the many big names out there.

I’ll add some fun pictures from my PhD here when I have time.
